question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
A person who renounces a religious or political belief or principle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Apostate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct one-word substitution is "Apostate" — a person who renounces or abandons a religious, political, or other belief or principle that they formerly held. (धर्म या सिद्धांत को त्यागने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He was branded an apostate by his former party after he publicly renounced its ideology.

• The related noun is "apostasy" — the act of abandoning one's religious or political faith or principles.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Arsonist (आगजनी करने वाला): A person who deliberately sets fire to property.

• Option 3: Anarchist (अराजकतावादी): A person who believes in the abolition of all government and law, favouring a stateless society.

• Option 4: Agnostic (अज्ञेयवादी): A person who believes that nothing is known or can be known about the existence of God; one who neither affirms nor denies religious belief.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Apostate" (one who abandons a belief) with "Atheist" (one who does not believe in God at all) or "Agnostic" (one who is unsure/non-committal about God's existence).

• Other commonly asked one-word substitutions for people and belief: Zealot (a fanatically committed person), Bigot (an intolerant person), Iconoclast (one who attacks cherished beliefs/traditions).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Dead lock
option_2: A state in which progress is impossible
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A state in which progress is impossible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom/phrase "Deadlock" means a situation, typically one involving opposing parties, in which no progress can be made because neither side is willing to change its position. (गतिरोध — जब आगे बढ़ना असंभव हो जाए)
◦ Example: The negotiations between the two countries reached a deadlock and no agreement could be signed.

• The word is formed from "dead" (without life/movement) + "lock" (a fixed, immovable state), together suggesting a complete standstill.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To be anxious is the meaning of idioms like "to be on tenterhooks" or "to have butterflies in one's stomach", not "deadlock".

• Option 3: To lose an important asset is closer to the meaning of an idiom such as "to lose one's crown jewels", unrelated to "deadlock".

• Option 4: To attract is the meaning of expressions like "to catch someone's eye", not "deadlock".

NOTE

• Related idioms of stalemate/impasse: "To reach a stalemate", "To hit a wall", and "To be at a standstill" — all describe situations where no further progress can be made.

• Do not confuse "deadlock" (a standoff between parties) with "dead heat" (a tie in a race/competition).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sliede.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 3 is spelt incorrectly. The correct spelling is "Slide" (S-L-I-D-E), not "Sliede".

• Spelling key: the letters are S + L + I + D + E, in that exact order — note that the "I" is immediately followed by "D"; there is no extra "E" between them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Brinjal" is spelt correctly — a vegetable, also called eggplant/aubergine.

• Option 2: "Mouse" is spelt correctly — a small rodent, or the computer pointing device.

• Option 4: "Blink" is spelt correctly — to shut and open the eyes quickly.

NOTE

• Words commonly confused by letter transposition in SSC spelling questions: "believe" (not beleive), "receive" (not recieve), "friend" (not freind), "field" (not feild) — remember the rule "i before e, except after c".

• Always read each option letter-by-letter rather than relying on how the word 'looks', since transposed-letter errors (like sliede/slide) are easy to miss at a glance.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
Fear of heights.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Acrophobia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct one-word substitution is "Acrophobia" — an extreme or irrational fear of heights. (ऊंचाई से डर)
◦ Example: He refused to go up the tower because of his acrophobia.

• The word is formed from the Greek "akron" (summit/height) + "phobos" (fear).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Agoraphobia (भीड़ या खुले स्थान का भय): Fear of open or crowded public spaces from which escape might be difficult.

• Option 2: Claustrophobia (बंद स्थान का भय): Fear of confined or enclosed spaces.

• Option 4: Homophobia (समलैंगिकता के प्रति पूर्वाग्रह): Dislike of or prejudice against homosexual people; strictly not a "fear of a place/thing" like the other options, but a social prejudice.

NOTE

• Other commonly asked phobia-related one-word substitutions: Xenophobia (fear/dislike of foreigners), Arachnophobia (fear of spiders), Nyctophobia (fear of the dark), and Hydrophobia (fear of water).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who loves mankind
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Philanthropist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct one-word substitution is "Philanthropist" — a person who seeks to promote the welfare of others, especially by donating money generously to good causes; one who loves mankind. (परोपकारी व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: The billionaire philanthropist donated most of his fortune to educational charities.

• The word comes from the Greek "philos" (loving) + "anthropos" (mankind).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Philistine (अरसिक व्यक्ति): A person who is hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts.

• Option 2: Philologist (भाषाविज्ञानी): A person who studies the structure, historical development, and relationships of languages.

• Option 3: Philanderer (स्त्रीलोलुप व्यक्ति): A man who engages in numerous casual sexual relationships with women.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the "phil-" (loving) root words: Philanthropist (loves mankind), Philatelist (loves/collects stamps), Philologist (loves language), Bibliophile (loves books), Anglophile (loves England/English things).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Quail
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cringe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Quail", when used as a verb, means to feel or show fear or apprehension; to flinch or shrink back timidly, which is closest in meaning to "Cringe". (डर के मारे सिकुड़ जाना/पीछे हटना)
◦ Example: She quailed at the thought of speaking in front of such a large audience.

• Note that "quail" is also a noun meaning a small game bird, but in synonym-based SSC questions it is tested in its verb sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Approach (पास आना): To come near to someone or something; the opposite sense of drawing closer rather than shrinking back.

• Option 3: Assail (हमला करना): To attack someone or something violently; the aggressor's action, not the fearful reaction.

• Option 4: Tyrant (अत्याचारी): A cruel and oppressive ruler; a noun describing a person, not a feeling of fear.

NOTE

• Other words meaning "to shrink back in fear", often confused in SSC vocabulary questions: Cower, Flinch, Wince, Recoil, Blanch.

• Do not confuse "quail" (to cringe in fear) with "quell" (to suppress/put down, e.g. to quell a riot).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The efforts of the Government in providing health education and Primary Health Centres is borne fruits.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. have borne.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The efforts of the Government in providing health education and Primary Health Centres". The head noun of this subject is the plural noun "efforts", so the verb must agree with a plural subject.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with Present Perfect Tense: with a plural subject, the auxiliary verb used is "have", followed by the past participle (V3) of the main verb — have + V3. The past participle of "bear" (in the sense of "to produce/yield") is "borne".

• Applying the rule: plural subject "efforts" + "have" + past participle "borne" → "...Primary Health Centres have borne fruits."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "has borne" is incorrect because "has" is a singular auxiliary and does not agree with the plural subject "efforts".

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "is borne" wrongly uses the singular present-tense auxiliary "is" with a plural subject, so the sentence as printed is not grammatically correct.

• Option 4: "was bore" is incorrect on two counts — "was" is a singular past-tense auxiliary that does not match the plural subject, and "bore" is the simple past form of "bear", not its past participle (which is required after an auxiliary verb like "was/have").

NOTE

• "Bear" has two different past participles depending on meaning: "borne" is used in the general sense (to carry, endure, produce/yield — e.g. "the tree has borne fruit"), while "born" is used only in the passive sense of birth (e.g. "the child was born").

• Always identify the true head noun of a long subject phrase before checking subject-verb agreement — prepositional phrases like "of the Government" or "in providing..." do not affect the number of the verb.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: A welcoming voice from the open dorway.
option_2: A welcoming voice from the open doorway.
option_3: A welcoming voise from the open doorway.
option_4: A welcomng voice from the open doorway.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A welcoming voice from the open doorway.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 2 is the only sentence in which all the words are spelt correctly: "welcoming", "voice", and "doorway" are all spelt as per standard English spelling.

• Spelling keys: "doorway" = door + way (no missing letters); "voice" has the order v-o-i-c-e; "welcoming" has the order w-e-l-c-o-m-i-n-g.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dorway" is incorrect — the "o" after "d" is missing; it should be "doorway".

• Option 3: "voise" is incorrect — the ending should be "-ce", not "-se"; the correct spelling is "voice".

• Option 4: "welcomng" is incorrect — the "i" before "ng" is missing; it should be "welcoming".

NOTE

• Compare each option word by word rather than reading the sentence for meaning, since spelling-error questions typically hide just one silently dropped or swapped letter in an otherwise correct-looking word.

• Commonly misspelt "-ing" words in SSC exams: beginning, occurring, referring, travelling — all involve doubling or retaining letters that are easy to drop.

question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, then select the option "No error".
We talked about writing a will, but it/ was one of those thing you never/ get around to doing.
option_1: was one of those thing you never
option_4: We talked about writing a will, but it
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. was one of those thing you never.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "was one of those thing you never". The demonstrative adjective "those" is a plural determiner and must be followed by a plural noun.

• Rule — Demonstrative Agreement: "this/that" are used with singular nouns, while "these/those" are used with plural nouns (e.g. "those things", not "those thing").

• Applying the rule: since "those" is used, the noun must be the plural "things", not the singular "thing" — the correct segment should read "was one of those things you never".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain a grammatical error, as explained above.

• Option 3: "get around to doing." is incorrect because this segment is grammatically correct — "get around to doing (something)" is a standard idiomatic construction meaning "to find time to do something eventually".

• Option 4: "We talked about writing a will, but it" is incorrect because this segment contains no grammatical error; it correctly sets up the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly tested determiner-noun agreement pairs in SSC error-spotting: this book / these books, that child / those children, each student (singular) / all students (plural), a few problems / little water.

• The idiom "to get around to (doing) something" means to finally find the time or motivation to do a task one has been putting off.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct passive form of the sentence.
Daniel and Mary invited us to their wedding.
option_1: We have been invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.
option_2: We were invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.
option_3: We are invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.
option_4: We had been invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. We were invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Daniel and Mary invited us to their wedding" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "us" becomes the subject "We"; being plural, the auxiliary used is "were"; the verb "invited" (already in V3 form, since "invite" is a regular verb) is retained; and "to their wedding" is retained (with "their" changing to "Daniel and Mary's").
◦ Passive: We were invited to Daniel and Mary's wedding.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "We have been invited..." is incorrect because "have been + V3" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 3: "We are invited..." is incorrect because "are + V3" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 4: "We had been invited..." is incorrect because "had been + V3" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• When the by-agent is a proper noun possessive (e.g. "Daniel and Mary"), and it forms part of a noun phrase like "wedding" that is retained rather than converted into a "by + agent" phrase, the possessive form (Daniel and Mary's) is kept as is.

• Always first identify the tense of the active sentence correctly before choosing the passive auxiliary — a common trap is picking the wrong tense's passive structure.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Many people
P. learn better when they have something tangible
Q. hold in their hands and get their head
R. to work with, a physical object they can
S. round and low-cost 3D printers make that possible
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. PRQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence starts with the fixed opening "Many people", which must be followed logically by a verb phrase describing what many people do.

• Part P ("learn better when they have something tangible") logically follows "Many people", giving "Many people learn better when they have something tangible".

• Part R ("to work with, a physical object they can") follows P, completing the idea of "tangible... to work with", and introducing the relative clause "a physical object they can...".

• Part Q ("hold in their hands and get their head") naturally continues the relative clause begun in R — "a physical object they can hold in their hands and get their head...".

• Part S ("round and low-cost 3D printers make that possible") completes the idiomatic phrase "get their head round" (meaning to understand something) and adds the concluding independent clause about 3D printers.

• Reading the full sentence in order P-R-Q-S: "Many people learn better when they have something tangible to work with, a physical object they can hold in their hands and get their head round, and low-cost 3D printers make that possible" — a complete, logically connected sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (PRSQ) is incorrect because it places S ("round and low-cost 3D printers make that possible") before Q ("hold in their hands..."), breaking the idiom "get their head round" and the logical flow.

• Option 3 (QPRS) is incorrect because it starts with Q ("hold in their hands and get their head"), which cannot directly follow "Many people" as it lacks a proper connecting verb at the start.

• Option 4 (QRSP) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3 — Q cannot begin the sentence after "Many people", and the resulting order does not form a coherent sentence.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-jumble questions, always locate the part containing the main verb that can directly follow the fixed opening phrase — this is usually the correct starting part.

• The idiom "to get one's head round something" means to understand or come to terms with something, especially something difficult or confusing.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Opaque
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Arcane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Besides its literal sense of "not transparent", the word "Opaque" is also used figuratively to mean hard to understand, unclear, or obscure. Among the given options, "Arcane" — meaning mysterious, secret, or understood by only a very few people — is closest to this figurative sense of obscurity. (रहस्यमय/दुर्बोध)
◦ Example: The legal jargon in the contract was so opaque/arcane that even the lawyers struggled to explain it.

• Both words describe something that is not easily grasped or seen through, whether literally (light) or figuratively (meaning).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Unadulterated (शुद्ध/मिलावट रहित): Pure, not mixed or diluted with anything else — unrelated to the idea of obscurity.

• Option 2: Translucent (पारभासी): Allowing light to pass through partially — in fact nearly opposite in literal meaning to "opaque".

• Option 3: Clear (स्पष्ट): Transparent or easy to understand — the direct opposite (antonym) of "opaque", not a synonym.

NOTE

• "Opaque" has two senses commonly tested by SSC: (i) literal — not transparent (antonym: transparent, translucent, clear); (ii) figurative — hard to understand (synonym: obscure, arcane, cryptic, abstruse).

• Other words meaning "difficult to understand/mysterious": Cryptic, Abstruse, Enigmatic, Esoteric, Recondite.

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below.
Frighten
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Reassure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Frighten" means to make someone afraid or anxious; its antonym is "Reassure", which means to say or do something to remove someone's doubts or fears and restore their confidence. (आश्वस्त करना)
◦ Example: The doctor's calm explanation reassured the frightened patient.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Startle (चौंकाना): To cause someone to feel sudden shock or alarm — a synonym of "frighten", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Petrify (भयभीत कर देना): To make someone so frightened that they are unable to move or think — again a synonym, meaning to terrify.

• Option 3: Alarm (सतर्क/भयभीत करना): To make someone anxious or aware of danger — also a synonym of "frighten".

NOTE

• All three incorrect options (Startle, Petrify, Alarm) are actually near-synonyms of "Frighten" — a common SSC trap where three options belong to the same meaning-family as the given word, and only one is the true opposite.

• Other synonyms of "frighten": Terrify, Scare, Intimidate, Unnerve, Daunt. Other antonyms: Comfort, Calm, Soothe, Embolden.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Obliquity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Opacity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Obliquity" means indirectness or lack of straightforwardness in speech, thought, or conduct; a deviation from what is clear, direct, or morally straightforward. In this sense of unclearness/indirectness, it is closest to "Opacity" — the state of being difficult to see through or understand; obscurity. (अस्पष्टता/दुर्बोधता)
◦ Example: The obliquity/opacity of his answer left everyone unsure of what he actually meant.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Profundity (गहनता): Great depth of insight or knowledge — describes intellectual depth, not indirectness/obscurity.

• Option 2: Incisiveness (पैनापन): The quality of being sharp, clear, and direct in expressing thought — nearly opposite to the indirectness implied by "obliquity".

• Option 3: Surety (निश्चितता/जमानत): Certainty, or a person who takes responsibility for another's obligation — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• "Oblique" (adjective) has both a literal sense (slanting, not straight/perpendicular) and a figurative sense (indirect, evasive) — SSC vocabulary questions usually test the figurative sense.

• Words related to indirectness/obscurity often confused in SSC: Ambiguity, Vagueness, Equivocation, Circumlocution.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. elderly is on the increase, and, although they constitute only
Q. a small minority of the retired population, their
R. in all advanced industrial societies the proportion of infirm
S. claim on social services is disproportionately heavy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. RPQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part R ("in all advanced industrial societies the proportion of infirm") is the most logical opening part, since it introduces the subject and setting of the sentence — "in all advanced industrial societies, the proportion of infirm...".

• Part P ("elderly is on the increase, and, although they constitute only") follows R, completing the noun phrase "the proportion of infirm elderly" and adding the main verb "is on the increase".

• Part Q ("a small minority of the retired population, their") follows P, completing the concessive clause begun by "although they constitute only..." with "a small minority of the retired population".

• Part S ("claim on social services is disproportionately heavy") concludes the sentence, completing "their claim on social services is disproportionately heavy".

• Reading the full sentence in order R-P-Q-S: "In all advanced industrial societies the proportion of infirm elderly is on the increase, and, although they constitute only a small minority of the retired population, their claim on social services is disproportionately heavy" — a complete, logically coherent sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PSRQ) is incorrect because it starts with P ("elderly is on the increase..."), which cannot begin the sentence as there is no subject/context established for "elderly" yet.

• Option 2 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it places S directly after R, disrupting the noun phrase "the proportion of infirm elderly" which must be completed by P before moving to the "although" clause.

• Option 3 (QPSR) is incorrect because it starts with Q ("a small minority of the retired population, their"), which cannot logically begin the sentence.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, look for parts that must grammatically complete another part's incomplete phrase (e.g. "the proportion of infirm" + "elderly") — these pairs are usually inseparable and help eliminate wrong options quickly.

• The correlative structure "although... their..." signals a concessive clause followed by a main clause, which helps identify the Q-S sequence at the end.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Method to my madness
option_1: Someone who is unpredictable and can cause damage if not kept in check.
option_3: To state a fact so that there are no doubts or objections.
option_4: Strange or crazy actions that appear meaningless but in the end are done for a good reason.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Strange or crazy actions that appear meaningless but in the end are done for a good reason.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Method to my/his/her madness" means that seemingly strange, illogical, or crazy behaviour actually has an underlying purpose, plan, or reasoning behind it. (पागलपन के पीछे भी एक तरकीब/उद्देश्य होना)
◦ Example: He rearranges his desk in a way that looks chaotic, but there is method to his madness — he can find anything in seconds.

• The phrase originates from Shakespeare's Hamlet, where Polonius remarks of Hamlet's odd behaviour, "Though this be madness, yet there is method in't."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Someone who is unpredictable and can cause damage if not kept in check" describes a "loose cannon", not this idiom.

• Option 2: "To get someone drunk" is unrelated; this could loosely describe idioms like "to ply someone with drink", not "method to my madness".

• Option 3: "To state a fact so that there are no doubts or objections" describes an idiom like "to put it beyond doubt" or "to state categorically", not this one.

NOTE

• Other Shakespeare-derived idioms commonly tested by SSC: "Break the ice" (Taming of the Shrew), "Wild goose chase" (Romeo and Juliet), "In a pickle" (The Tempest), "Heart of gold" (Henry V).

• Related idiom: "There's a method in the madness" — used interchangeably with "method to my/his madness".

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
People that are lonely have higher levels of the hormone cortisol.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. People that are lonely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the use of the relative pronoun "that" to refer to the plural human antecedent "People".

• Rule — Relative Pronouns for Persons: the relative pronoun "who" (or "whom" for the object case) is used for people, while "that" or "which" is generally used for things, animals, or when "who" is not the most idiomatic/precise choice. In formal written English tested by SSC, "who" is preferred over "that" when referring to a class of people such as "people".

• Applying the rule: "People that are lonely" should correctly read "People who are lonely".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "have higher levels of" is incorrect because this segment contains no grammatical error — subject-verb agreement (plural "People" + "have") is correct.

• Option 3: "the hormone cortisol." is incorrect because this noun phrase is grammatically and factually fine, correctly naming the hormone in apposition.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain an error, as explained above.

NOTE

• While "that" is sometimes used informally for people (especially in restrictive clauses), SSC exams consistently test the formal rule that "who/whom" is the correct relative pronoun for persons.

• Relative pronoun usage: who/whom — persons; which — things/animals; that — persons, things, or animals (informal/restrictive, but avoided for people in formal SSC usage); whose — possessive, for persons or things.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
She dedicated her entire life to the serviced of the poorest of the poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. service of the poorest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "serviced of the poorest" wrongly uses "serviced" (the past tense/participle of the verb "to service", meaning to maintain or repair) where a noun is required after the article "the" and before the preposition "of".

• Rule: the structure **"dedicated her life to the ___ of the poor" requires a noun in the blank, not a verb form. The correct noun form here is "service"** (meaning the act of helping or serving others).

• Applying the rule: "dedicated her entire life to the service of the poorest of the poor" is the grammatically correct construction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain a clear error — "serviced" is a verb form wrongly used as a noun.

• Option 3: "services off the poorest" is incorrect because "off" is the wrong preposition; it should be "of", and "services" (plural) does not fit as naturally as the standard idiomatic phrase "the service of".

• Option 4: "serviced of the poorer" is incorrect because it retains the wrong word "serviced" and also changes "poorest" (superlative, correct in context of "of the poor") to "poorer" (comparative), which is grammatically unnecessary here.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "service" (noun: the act of helping; or verb: to formally serve) with "serviced" (past tense of the verb "to service", used mainly for maintaining machines/vehicles, e.g. "the car was serviced").

• The phrase "the poorest of the poor" is a fixed idiomatic superlative expression meaning "the most destitute among poor people", commonly seen in SSC reading passages.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
"I have heard the podcast before," Nita says.
option_1: Nita says that she is hearing the podcast before.
option_2: Nita says that she had heard the podcast before.
option_3: Nita says that she has heard the podcast before.
option_4: Nita says that she had heard the podcast ago.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Nita says that she has heard the podcast before.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reporting verb in the given sentence is "says", which is in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Narration with a Present-Tense Reporting Verb: when the reporting verb (says/says that) is in the present tense, the tense of the reported speech does NOT change in the indirect form — it is retained exactly as in the direct speech.

• Applying the rule: the direct speech "I have heard the podcast before" is in the Present Perfect Tense, so it remains in the Present Perfect Tense in indirect speech, with the pronoun "I" changing to "she" (referring to Nita).
◦ Indirect: Nita says that she has heard the podcast before.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Nita says that she is hearing the podcast before" is incorrect because it wrongly converts the tense to Present Continuous, and "is hearing... before" is not grammatically coherent since "before" implies a completed past action, not an ongoing one.

• Option 2: "Nita says that she had heard the podcast before" is incorrect because the tense is wrongly changed to Past Perfect, which is unnecessary since the reporting verb "says" is in the present tense.

• Option 4: "Nita says that she had heard the podcast ago" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 (wrong tense change to Past Perfect), and additionally uses "ago", which is not idiomatically used with "had heard... before" in this construction.

NOTE

• Tense-change rules in narration apply only when the reporting verb is in the past tense; if the reporting verb is in the present or future tense, the tense of the reported speech remains unchanged.

• Time expressions like "before" typically stay the same in indirect speech (unlike "ago", which is often used only in direct speech and may change to "before" when the reporting verb is in the past tense).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
The _______ of revenge demanded a life for a life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. obligations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence **"The _______ of revenge demanded a life for a life" requires a noun that conveys a strong sense of duty or moral compulsion associated with the concept of "revenge". "Obligations"** — meaning duties or moral/legal requirements that one is bound to fulfil — fits this sense perfectly: the (perceived) duty of revenge demanded that a life be repaid with a life.

• Contextually, phrases like "blood obligation" or "the obligation of revenge/honour" are commonly used to describe a code of conduct that compels retributive action.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "cheering" means shouting in approval or encouragement — it does not fit the serious, duty-bound tone of the sentence about revenge demanding a life.

• Option 2: "moaning" means making a low, mournful sound expressing pain or complaint — it does not convey the sense of a binding duty required by the context.

• Option 3: "crowning" means the act of placing a crown on someone, or (as "crowing") boastful triumph — neither fits the meaning of a compelling duty in the sentence.

NOTE

• In fill-in-the-blank vocabulary questions, always check which option best matches the overall tone and logical cause-effect relationship of the sentence, not just individual word meanings in isolation.

• Words related to duty/compulsion often tested by SSC: obligation, compulsion, duty, imperative, mandate.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Social media platforms and many people on them have their own (1)_______ and they are often trying to sell you things. So, be (2) ______ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users and think about (3) ______ they want from you when engaging.To gauge which uses are positive and (4) ______ and which are detrimental, ask yourself simply, when does using social media make me feel good or bad, and why? Do I (5) ______use it all of the time?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. agendas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun describing what social media platforms and people on them "have their own" of, in the context of "often trying to sell you things". "Agendas" — meaning hidden or personal plans/purposes behind one's actions — fits this context perfectly, since the passage goes on to warn that platforms/people often have an underlying purpose (selling things) behind their online presence.

• The phrase "have their own agenda" is a common collocation meaning to have a private motive or plan, often self-serving.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "steam" does not fit; "steam" relates to vapour or (idiomatically) energy/momentum ("run out of steam"), unrelated to platforms having a purpose.

• Option 3: "excuses" means reasons given to justify a fault, which does not logically fit "have their own excuses... and they are often trying to sell you things" — there is no fault being excused here.

• Option 4: "considerations" means factors taken into account when making a decision; it does not fit as naturally as "agendas" in the sense of a hidden self-interested purpose.

NOTE

• The collocation "hidden agenda" or "have an agenda" is frequently tested in SSC cloze passages relating to media, politics, or persuasion.

• Cloze passages often require choosing the word that best fits the overall tone/argument of the passage, not just literal dictionary meaning — always read the full passage before finalising a blank.

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Social media platforms and many people on them have their own (1)_______ and they are often trying to sell you things. So, be (2) ______ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users and think about (3) ______ they want from you when engaging.To gauge which uses are positive and (4) ______ and which are detrimental, ask yourself simply, when does using social media make me feel good or bad, and why? Do I (5) ______use it all of the time?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. aware.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an adjective meaning conscious or mindful, matching the sense of "be _____ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users". "Aware" — meaning having knowledge or perception of a situation or fact — fits perfectly with the collocation "be aware of".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "aroused" means stimulated or awakened (often of feelings or interest); "be aroused of" is not idiomatic English.

• Option 2: "valiant" means possessing or showing courage; it does not collocate meaningfully with "of how much time and energy you give".

• Option 3: "calm" means free from agitation; "be calm of" is not standard idiomatic usage — "calm about" would be closer, but the meaning still does not fit as well as "aware", since the passage is about monitoring/noticing time and energy spent, not staying calm about it.

NOTE

• The fixed collocation "be aware of" is one of the most frequently tested adjective + preposition patterns in SSC cloze/fill-in-the-blank questions.

• Other common adjective + "of" collocations: conscious of, fond of, capable of, afraid of, proud of, aware of.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Social media platforms and many people on them have their own (1)_______ and they are often trying to sell you things. So, be (2) ______ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users and think about (3) ______ they want from you when engaging.To gauge which uses are positive and (4) ______ and which are detrimental, ask yourself simply, when does using social media make me feel good or bad, and why? Do I (5) ______use it all of the time?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. what.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank fits into the clause **"think about _____ they want from you when engaging", which requires an interrogative/relative pronoun that can head a noun clause functioning as the object of "think about". "What"** correctly introduces this noun clause, meaning "think about [the thing] they want from you".

• Rule: "what" is used as a pronoun meaning "that which" or "the thing(s) that", commonly introducing noun clauses after verbs like think about, know, wonder, ask, etc.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that" cannot correctly introduce this noun clause here because "think about that they want from you" is not grammatically acceptable — "that" cannot function as the object pronoun of "want" within the clause the way "what" does.

• Option 2: "whilst" is a conjunction meaning "while" (used to show two things happening at the same time), which does not fit grammatically in this position at all.

• Option 3: "which" is normally used with a specific antecedent already mentioned (a relative pronoun), whereas here no specific antecedent noun exists for "which" to refer back to — "what" is required to mean "the thing(s) that".

NOTE

• "What" is used as a "fused relative" pronoun combining the antecedent and the relative pronoun together — equivalent to "the thing(s) that" — very commonly tested in SSC cloze and error-spotting questions.

• Do not confuse "what" (no antecedent, self-contained) with "which" (requires an antecedent already named in the sentence).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Social media platforms and many people on them have their own (1)_______ and they are often trying to sell you things. So, be (2) ______ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users and think about (3) ______ they want from you when engaging.To gauge which uses are positive and (4) ______ and which are detrimental, ask yourself simply, when does using social media make me feel good or bad, and why? Do I (5) ______use it all of the time?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. productive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an adjective that pairs with "positive" (via "and") to contrast with "detrimental" later in the same sentence: **"which uses are positive and _____ and which are detrimental". "Productive"** — meaning producing good or useful results/benefits — logically contrasts with "detrimental" (harmful) and complements "positive".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "pliable" means easily bent or influenced/adaptable; it does not form a natural positive contrast with "detrimental" in this context.

• Option 2: "possessive" means having or showing a strong desire to control or own something; it carries a negative connotation and does not pair naturally with "positive" as a good quality of social media use.

• Option 3: "punitive" means inflicting or intended as punishment; this is a negative quality, which would not logically be grouped with "positive" uses as opposed to "detrimental" ones.

NOTE

• In this sentence, the passage sets up a clear semantic contrast: positive/productive (good) vs. detrimental (bad) — always look for such contrast/parallel clues in cloze passages to identify the word that logically completes the intended meaning.

• Words in the "beneficial" family often tested together: productive, beneficial, constructive, wholesome, fruitful — versus their opposites detrimental, harmful, counterproductive, destructive.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Social media platforms and many people on them have their own (1)_______ and they are often trying to sell you things. So, be (2) ______ of how much time and energy you give to sellers and users and think about (3) ______ they want from you when engaging.To gauge which uses are positive and (4) ______ and which are detrimental, ask yourself simply, when does using social media make me feel good or bad, and why? Do I (5) ______use it all of the time?

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. need to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank fits into the question **"Do I _____ use it all of the time?", which, following the auxiliary "Do", requires a bare-infinitive-compatible phrase that logically questions necessity of constant use. "Need to"** correctly forms the phrase "Do I need to use it...", questioning whether continuous use is actually necessary.

• Rule: after the auxiliary "Do" in a question, the following verb phrase must be in its base form; "need to" functions here as a semi-modal verb phrase meaning "to be necessary/obliged to".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "could" is a modal verb and cannot correctly follow the auxiliary "Do" in a question — modals do not take "do-support" (e.g. "Do I could use it" is ungrammatical; it should simply be "Could I use it?").

• Option 3: "ought to" is also a modal-type expression that does not take "do-support" — the grammatically correct form would be "Ought I to use it?", not "Do I ought to use it".

• Option 4: "must" is a modal verb and, like "could" and "ought to", cannot grammatically follow "Do" — the correct form would be "Must I use it?", not "Do I must use it".

NOTE

• "Need" can function either as a modal verb (no "-s", no "do-support", e.g. "Need I say more?") or as an ordinary/semi-modal verb (takes "-s", uses "do-support", e.g. "Does he need to go?", "Do I need to..."). In this sentence, since "Do" is already used, "need to" (ordinary verb usage) is required, not the modal "need".

• True modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to) never take "do-support" in standard questions/negatives.
